name: Mint
lede: Mint is the pale, cool green of the herb's leaves, a pastel that has come to mean freshness and cleanliness.

sections.title: The leaf and the pastel
sections.body:
Paterson defines mint-green as the green of the leaves of the aromatic plant, a pastel green [1]. The X11 set has MintCream, a near-white with a green breath, with the hex code #F5FFFA [2]. See [[mint-cream]] for that one. The same dictionary calls Kelly green a strong mint green, which shows how far the word stretches [3].

Mint was among the leading plants in the medieval pharmacopoeia, according to Pastoureau, so the plant was long tied to medicine before it named a color [4].

sections.title: Why mint reads as clean
sections.body:
Pastoureau argues that green now cleans, refreshes and purifies, in the image of mint and menthol products, and links this to hygiene, health and sport [5]. Batchelor, describing American suburbs, lists frosted mint among the house colors, beside petal pink, buttercup and lilac [6]. A grower of naturally colored cotton, in Finlay's account, found a boll of aqua green that mixed sea turquoise with moss and mint [7].

On a screen, mint sits between [[pastel-green]] and [[light-green]], and is bluer and softer than [[green]] [8].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The name is recorded in Maerz and Paul (1930), the ISCC-NBS system (1955) and the xkcd survey (2010) [8]. Our archive holds 1 painting that matches, dated 1825, as photographed, so mint is almost absent from painting [9]. The printed word peaks in the 1810s, but that counts every sense, including the herb and the coin-making place, so it is a weak guide to the color [9].

origin.first_recorded: Maerz and Paul, 1930 (earliest in our sources)
